title: Sources and authenticity
intro: Where the material on this site comes from, what its licence allows, and how much weight it can carry. Nothing here is presented as more settled than it is.

items.name: Hora
items.covers: Predictive or natal astrology - reading a birth chart. This is the branch of the Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra and of almost everything on this site.

items.name: Siddhanta
items.covers: Mathematical astronomy - planetary positions, motions, distances and strengths. The ephemeris and the ascendant calculation on this site belong here.

items.name: Samhita
items.covers: Mundane astrology - collective matters, weather, society. Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita is the standard work. Not covered on this site.

bphs.title: About the Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra
bphs.note: This is the text most often cited as the authority for the rules on this site, so its standing matters.
facts: It is the most comprehensive surviving shastra on Vedic natal astrology, and is ascribed to the sage Parashara.
The version in common circulation has 97 chapters. That numbering follows R. Santhanam's 1984 English translation, which is itself in copyright.
The origin and date of the original composition are unknown.

J. Gonda dates the purva-khanda (the first part) to roughly 600-750 CE. He notes it is deeply indebted to Varahamihira's Brihat Jataka, which is earlier, and that it borrows verses from Sphujidhvaja. The uttara-khanda was commented on by Govindasvamin around 850 CE.
Bhattotpala, writing around 900 CE, recorded that although he had heard of the Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra he had never seen it. The text appears to have been lost for about nine hundred years.
Manuscripts re-emerged only in the early twentieth century. The first printed version was in 1905, from the Sri Venkateswara Press.
No ancient commentary on the text is known. The oldest known is Devacandra Jha's Hindi commentary from the first half of the twentieth century - less than a hundred years old.
Sitaram Jha's 1944 edition reportedly admitted that he had changed and removed elements of the manuscript.

The practical consequence: when a modern book says 'Parashara says', it is usually quoting a twentieth-century reconstruction of a text whose early history is genuinely uncertain. Treat the rules as the living tradition's, not as a verbatim ancient authority.

howto.title: How to read this
howto.note: Original notes, not quoted from any source.
points: The calculation is the factual part. A planet's longitude, a nakshatra pada, the ascendant - these are computed and can be checked. The meaning attached to them is the tradition's, and reasonable astrologers disagree about it.

Astrology here is a traditional interpretive framework, not an established science. Nothing on this site is a prediction of a specific event, and nothing here should be used to make a decision you would not otherwise make.

A chart does not remove your choices. The classical texts treat daivam - fate - as one factor among several, alongside effort, and the older literature is much more insistent on effort than modern popular astrology is.

Scores and doshas are inputs, not verdicts. The 36-point matching total, Mangal dosha, Kaal Sarp - the texts themselves treat these as things to reason about, and most of them have classical cancellation rules that this site deliberately does not apply. Treat a bare score as the beginning of a question, not the answer.
Read a chart from the Moon when the birth time is uncertain. That is the standard fallback, and it is why the Moon columns are shown alongside the lagna ones.

Be careful with anyone who is certain. A reading that names dates and guarantees outcomes, or that creates fear to sell a remedy, is not doing what the texts describe. The older literature is explicit that an astrologer should be learned, steady and unwilling to frighten people.
Remedies here are faith practice. A mantra, a daan or a havan is a religious act. It is not a substitute for a doctor, a lawyer or a financial adviser.
